title: It has been discovered that 'adjusting to the shape' is crucial for pushing back an asteroid approaching Earth with a nuclear explosion, and that the effect of altering its orbit differs by about five times.
excerpt: The idea of using a nuclear explosion to deflect an asteroid heading towards Earth and avoid a collision is a familiar concept in science fiction movies. New research by Sandia National Laboratories in the United States has revealed that the effectiveness of altering the trajectory of a nuclear explosion varies greatly depending on the shape of the asteroid. Even with the same asteroid, the effect can differ by about five times depending on the direction in which the explosion's energy is directed. Asteroid defense hits a lump in the road – News Releaseshttps://newsreleases.sandia.gov/asteroid-defense-hits-a-lump-in-the-road/ A nuclear blast could save Earth from an asteroid, but there's a catch | ScienceDaily https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261106174532.htm As a countermeasure against asteroids approaching Earth, methods of altering their orbits by crashing spacecraft into them are being researched. In 2022, NASA conducted the 'DART' mission, which involved crashing a probe into the asteroid Dimorphos, and successfully altered the asteroid's orbit. NASA's 'DART' experiment, which aims to alter the orbit of an asteroid by crashing a spacecraft into it, has been found to have also changed the orbital period of a binary asteroid group. - GIGAZINE On the other hand, when a large asteroid is approaching or when there is limited time before impact, using a nuclear explosion to alter its orbit is also being considered. The powerful X-rays generated by the nuclear explosion would hit the asteroid's surface, rapidly heating and vaporizing the surface material. The reaction force of the vaporized material ejected into space would push the asteroid, changing its direction of travel. However, real asteroids are not always perfect spheres. Their surfaces are uneven, and some are elongated or irregularly shaped. Conventional simulations often treat asteroids as simple spheres, making it difficult to simultaneously and accurately calculate the effects of complex shapes and nuclear explosions. by NASA Therefore, a research team led by physicist Nathan Moore at Sandia National Laboratories combined two types of simulation techniques that calculate different physical phenomena. The newly developed calculation algorithm is more than 1600 times faster than conventional methods, and it is now possible to investigate the effects of X-rays in detail while taking into account the complex shape of the asteroid. When the research team conducted simulations of irradiating the same asteroid with X-rays from different directions, they found that the asteroid's velocity changed by 3.9 mm per second when irradiated from one direction, while the change was only 0.8 mm per second when irradiated from another direction. This shows that simply changing the direction from which the X-rays are applied resulted in approximately a five-fold difference in the effect of altering its orbit. Furthermore, simulations using another asteroid showed that the direction in which the X-rays were directed could result in a difference of up to 17 times in the change in its rotation speed. Moore stated, 'We expected that the direction of the X-rays would be important, but we were surprised by the magnitude of the effect.' The new simulation uses three-dimensional shape data of asteroids captured by probes and other devices to calculate the effects while varying the intensity of the explosion, the distance to the asteroid, and the direction from which the X-rays arrive. It can also examine the amount of material vaporizing on the asteroid's surface at different locations, and estimate surface damage in addition to changes in orbit and rotation. When considering countermeasures against asteroids, there is a risk that if the celestial body is broken into smaller pieces, multiple fragments could collide with Earth. The research team explains that detailed simulations are crucial to keep the asteroid as intact as possible and move it in a safe direction. However, the new calculation method also has its limitations. While it can calculate the fracture of rocks on the asteroid's surface, it cannot accurately predict whether the entire asteroid will shatter. Furthermore, the calculation requires detailed shape data obtained by observing the asteroid from various angles, and it is not guaranteed that enough information will be collected before it collides with Earth. Moore stated, 'If you choose the right side, it will be successful, but if you aim wrong, it will be disastrous.' The research team plans to further improve their calculation methods so that they can determine the strength, location, and direction of the explosion based on the shape of the asteroid, which will help in considering ways to prevent future asteroid collisions.
